result.summary: Pindar celebrates Melissos of Thebes, victor in the pankration at the Isthmus and earlier in the chariot-race at Nemea. He praises the Kleonymid clan, its losses in war and its revival, and compares the small but fierce Melissos to Herakles overcoming Antaios.

scenes.title: Editor's introduction
scenes.summary: The editor discusses the uncertain date, the clan's losses and Melissos' victories.

scenes.title: Praise of Melissos and his clan
scenes.summary: Pindar praises restraint in fortune, Zeus as the source of excellence, and Melissos' two victories. He recalls the old fame of the Kleonymidai.
scenes.stakes: Good fortune can be lost through insolence and the changes of time.

scenes.title: War losses and revival
scenes.summary: The clan lost four men in war but now blossoms again through Poseidon's grace and earlier chariot wins at Athens and Sikyon.
scenes.stakes: The family's glory had fallen asleep after the loss of four men.

scenes.title: Aias and Homer's song
scenes.summary: Pindar cites Aias, whose excellence was preserved by Homer, and prays the Muses for similar song for Melissos.
scenes.stakes: Without poets, great deeds are forgotten.

scenes.title: Herakles against Antaios
scenes.summary: Melissos is likened to a lion and a fox, and to Herakles who came from Thebes to Libya to end Antaios' killings.
scenes.stakes: Herakles risks death wrestling the giant, who kills strangers.

scenes.title: Rites for Herakles' sons
scenes.summary: The Thebans honour Herakles and his eight sons with sacrifice and games, where Melissos won, guided by his trainer Orseas.

alias_notes.explanation: Epithet of Poseidon, god of the sea and earthquakes.

notable_quotes.reason: Pindar marks the pillars of Herakles as the limit of human achievement.
Expresses the poet's belief that well-spoken praise gives deeds undying fame.
Memorable portrait of a small athlete who is terrible in a grapple.

analysis.text: Success must be held with moderation, since fortune changes; poetry preserves excellence and renews a family's glory.
Victory odes were commissioned by aristocratic families, and Thebes' clan rivalry and war losses show the civic setting of athletic fame.

legacy.text: The pillars of Herakles as the limit of the known world became a lasting image, later reflected in the motto of 'Plus Ultra'.

fun_facts.text: The pankration was a combined wrestling and striking contest with almost no rules, so a small victor was notable.

language_notes.text: The battle of Plataiai (479 BC) was the decisive Greek land victory over the Persians; the editor suggests the ode alludes to it.
Pankration was a brutal combination of boxing and wrestling with very few rules.
"Restraineth" is an archaic third-person verb form; "besetting insolence" means the arrogance (hubris) that constantly attends success.
"The deep-chested lion" refers to the Nemean lion killed by Herakles; the "hollow vale" is Nemea, where Melissos won the chariot race.
The Labdakidai were descendants of Labdakos, an old royal house of Thebes, linked to Oedipus.
"Ways countless open unto me" means Pindar has endless routes for his song; the praise-subject gives him material.
The pillars of Herakles (Gibraltar) marked the western edge of the known world, so the phrase means the furthest limit of achievement.
"Shaker of Earth" is Poseidon's epithet, as god of earthquakes; Onchestos and the Isthmus (the "Bridge") were sites of his worship.
Games of Adrastos: funeral-style games at Sikyon, traditionally linked to the Argive king Adrastos, in which the family won chariot victories.
Aias killed himself after the Greeks awarded Achilles' armour to Ulysses instead of him; his suicide shames the Greeks who judged wrongly.
"Rod of his divine lays" pictures Homer's song as a staff or sceptre handing excellence on to later poets.
The fox "spreads out her feet" by rolling onto her back to meet the eagle's talons with her own claws.
Orion was the huge hunter of myth, a standard of great stature; Melissos is small by contrast.
Herakles, made immortal, married Hebe (goddess of youth), daughter of Hera.
"Pilot of his helm" calls the trainer Orseas a steersman; the footnote marks this as a metaphor for coaching.

context_notes.text: Antaios was a giant who gained strength from contact with the earth; Herakles defeated him by lifting him off the ground.
Zeus, king of the gods, was regarded as the ultimate giver of fortune and success.
Melissos proclaimed Thebes as his city, as winners' hometowns were announced by the herald.
Pindar refers to the clan's losses in war, probably fighting for Thebes, which he mourns before turning to its revival.
Antaios was a Libyan giant who forced strangers to wrestle and killed them; Herakles (son of Alkmene) defeated him.
Herakles' eight sons by Megara were, in myth, killed by him in madness; Thebes honoured them with annual rites at the Elektrai gates.

literary_notes.text: A general truth about change and human limits, typical of Pindar, sets mortal fortunes against the gods' immunity.
Changing gales driving men's lives compares fortune to shifting winds.
Reaching the ends of the earth exaggerates the clan's glory to show its extreme reach.
The abrupt command warns against overreaching, echoing the ode's theme of restraint.
War is a fierce snow-storm that leaves the family hearth desolate, picturing sudden, cold devastation.
The clan's revival is compared to earth blossoming with roses after winter, reversing the storm imagery.
The house's reawakened glory shines like the Morning-star among stars, with the house personified as a sleeper rising from bed.
Fame is an unquenchable light travelling over land and sea, expressing the poet's power to preserve deeds.
Melissos is compared to lions for courage and to a fox for cunning, praising both strength and skill.
Melissos' small size is paired with Herakles' defeat of Antaios, flattering him as a heroic underdog.
